source.title: VC Theoretical Explanation of Double Descent

page_placements.theme: Feature learning and fixed-feature limits differ by setting

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies network width and reports training and test error curves to model second descent, using VC bounds to interpret the curves. This bears on whether test error falls as width increases beyond interpolation, though the study says it is not replicating the original double-descent curves.
record.gate_note: The study reports width-sweep outcomes for random-feature classifiers and fully connected networks. The text describes the curves, while most curve values appear only in figures; results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own training- and test-error curves as network width increases, including a trained one-hidden-layer ReLU network and random-feature classifiers. These test V2 through a different training recipe and restricted binary-classification setting.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors argue that suitably configured VC bounds explain double descent, attributing second descent to near-zero training error with small weight norm. Their output-layer norm estimate for adaptive networks is a hypothesis restricted to second descent and separable, low-noise distributions. Superior performance over first-descent optima on large, clean datasets is an expectation, rather than a demonstrated general result.
record.recipe_differences: The study models double descent using VC bounds. It uses random-feature SVM and least-squares classifiers, and a restricted set of SGD-trained networks; it does not reproduce the listed original studies' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The text reports that label noise changes the curve shape and interpolation threshold; SVM's interpolation threshold rises with noise, while least-squares' is approximately the training-set size. It also reports different interpolation thresholds for SVM and least-squares.

fits_no_version.finding: At N=2000, random-feature least squares has 3.7% test error and output-weight norm squared 3.3, versus 3.1% and 2.3 for the adaptively trained network.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wide random-feature and adaptively trained networks can have similar output-weight norms and test errors on binary MNIST.

record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2023
record.problems: The adaptive-network VC-dimension estimate is presented as a hypothesis and is restricted to the second-descent region and well-separable, low-noise distributions. Most curve values are figure-only; the text provides no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on the tested version were left out. Figures 8–12 and 13–16 provide additional dataset or network settings, but their numeric curve values are figure-only; the text does not provide enough separately described results to extract further condition-specific rows without reading values from the figures.

untested.parts: No comparison establishes near-perfect fitting of fully random labels alongside above-chance natural-label generalization and chance random-label generalization.

The original unregularized, convergence-trained recipe and downsampled CIFAR-10 setting are not reproduced. The adaptive-network experiment considers only second descent, so it does not establish the interpolation-threshold peak.
No controlled convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or test of local connectivity, learned sparsity, or convolutional initialization.
No batch-size comparison under matched epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware perturbation measure, correlation with generalization gaps, or ranking against other measures. Output-weight norm is a different construct.
No removal and retraining experiment based on example memorization.

missing.what: Width sweeps for random Fourier features fitted with SVM and least squares. The text reports results similar to the random-ReLU experiments, but no row represents this feature-map condition.
Width sweeps with Gaussian pixel noise at standard deviations 0, 0.1 and 0.2. Record the classifier and noise conditions separately; numerical changes remain unavailable in the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: No challenges verdict is warranted. Label noise raises test error and flattens second descent, but the text still reports second descent; neither this nor poorer performance than a first-descent optimum establishes an absent or reversed post-interpolation width trend. Appendix Figures 8–16 are explicitly declared omitted in rows_left_out. The supplied text contains captions rather than readable plotted values, so numerical slopes, uncertainty, and exact interpolation behavior cannot be independently checked.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not compare fitting natural labels with fitting random labels.

The study does not test downsampled CIFAR-10 or isolate the interpolation-threshold peak as a double-descent claim. The random-feature experiments use SVM with C=64 or least squares, and the adaptive fully connected network is tested on binary MNIST digits.
The appendix reports a LeNet-5 width sweep, but does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks in a controlled test of their relative generalization or local connectivity.
The study uses output-layer weight norm squared as a proxy for VC dimension, not magnitude-aware sharpness or a ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
The study does not identify and remove memorized examples.
